question.question:
D1 — Retry scheduling: library hooks or a custom inline scheduler?
Project/branch/task: main branch, plan "Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md), touching 5 worker files.
ELI10: Your job library already knows how to retry a failed job later. The plan says: ignore that and write our own timer logic inside each of the 5 workers, because we want to pick the exact wait-time curve. Almost every job library lets you plug in your own curve through a hook, so you get the control without rebuilding scheduling, persistence of attempt counts, and the failed-job UI. Building it ourselves means five copies of code that has to survive worker crashes and restarts.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a hand-rolled scheduler that loses in-flight retries on worker restart or double-fires them, invisible in the library's dashboard; or, if the hook truly cannot express the curve, a library-bound design that needs a hack later.
Recommendation: A because the stated goal (a custom curve) is exactly what the backoff hook exists for [Layer 1], and the library already handles attempt persistence, dead-lettering and tooling.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (investigation only, approves nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library hook + custom curve (recommended) (human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Attempt count, next-run time and failed state persist in the library's store, so retries survive worker restarts
  ✅ The curve lives in one small function; dashboard, dead-letter and metrics come from the library for free
  ❌ If the installed library's hook cannot express the curve (unverified: library not in this repo), we fall back to B after a short delay
B) Custom inline scheduler (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min, plus ongoing maintenance)
  ✅ Total control over timing with no dependency on the library's hook semantics
  ✅ Works the same even if the library's retry feature is weak or absent
  ❌ Re-implements attempt persistence, restart safety and visibility; five copies to keep correct at 3am
C) Spike the hook first (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Removes the one real unknown (hook capability) before committing either way
  ✅ Cheap, and produces a concrete snippet to review
  ❌ Approves nothing and delays every downstream choice that depends on the mechanism

question.question:
D2 — Webhook delivery: what guarantee do receivers get once we retry?
Project/branch/task: main branch, plan "Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md), the `processWebhookJob()` rewrite.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if the job dies, the receiver gets nothing, but never two copies. Once we retry, a job that sent the webhook and then crashed before recording success will send it again. Receivers now have to cope with duplicates. The standard fix is to stamp every send with the same idempotency key across attempts so receivers can drop the second copy. The plan is silent on this.
Stakes if we pick wrong: duplicate webhooks trigger double side effects at receivers (double emails, double charges, double syncs), and the first support ticket arrives before anyone knows the guarantee changed.
Recommendation: A because at-least-once with a stable idempotency key is the standard contract for retried webhooks and costs one header plus a doc line.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) At-least-once + idempotency key (recommended) (human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Webhook failures are actually retried, and receivers have a documented way to drop duplicates
  ✅ Key derived from the job id, so it is stable across attempts with no new storage
  ❌ Receivers that ignore the header still see duplicates; the contract change must be communicated
B) Keep webhook at-most-once (opt out) (human: ~1 hour / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Zero behavior change for receivers; no contract to communicate
  ✅ Smallest diff for the webhook path; other 4 workers still gain retries
  ❌ Transient webhook failures stay lost, which is the problem the plan set out to fix
C) At-least-once, no key (as planned) (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ No extra work on the send path
  ✅ Receivers already deduping by payload are unaffected
  ❌ Silent contract change; receivers without dedup get duplicates and nothing tells them
Net: trading one header and a doc line against either lost webhooks or silent duplicates.

Con: receivers that ignore the header still see duplicates, so the contract change must be communicated. Effort human ~0.5 day / CC ~10 min. R1 fixed (D1); R3-R8 stay pending.

question.question:
D3 — How many times do we retry, and what happens when we give up?
Project/branch/task: main branch, plan "Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md), all 5 workers.
ELI10: Exponential backoff says how long to wait between tries, but not when to stop. Without a cap, a job whose dependency is permanently broken retries forever, and nobody is told. The usual answer is a maximum number of attempts, after which the job is parked in a failed set (dead-letter) and an alert fires so a human can look at it in the morning.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either zombie jobs that retry for days and quietly eat worker capacity, or jobs that silently vanish into a failed set nobody watches.
Recommendation: A because a cap plus an exhaustion alert is the only option where a permanently failing job becomes a visible, bounded event.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Cap 5 attempts + dead-letter + alert (recommended) (human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Every job's retry cost is bounded and exhaustion becomes a visible metric per worker
  ✅ Dead-lettered jobs are inspectable and replayable from the library's failed set
  ❌ One more metric/alert to wire into the existing monitoring stack
B) Cap 5 attempts, library default on exhaustion (human: ~1 hour / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Retry cost is bounded with almost no extra code beyond a config value
  ✅ Failed jobs still land in the library's failed set for manual inspection
  ❌ Nobody is told when jobs are exhausted; the failed set grows unwatched
C) No cap, as planned (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ No config or monitoring work at all
  ✅ A job eventually succeeds if the dependency ever recovers
  ❌ Permanently broken jobs retry forever, consuming worker slots with no signal
Net: trading one metric and a config value against unbounded or invisible failure.

options.label: Cap 5 attempts + dead-letter + alert (recommended)
options.description: Set a maximum attempt count per worker type, default 5, configurable. When a job exhausts its attempts it lands in the library's failed/dead-letter set and a `job_retries_exhausted` metric/alert fires carrying the worker name and job id. Every job's retry cost is bounded, exhaustion is visible per worker, and dead-lettered jobs are inspectable and replayable. Con: one more metric/alert to wire into the existing monitoring stack. Effort human ~0.5 day / CC ~10 min. R1, R2 fixed (D1, D2); R4-R8 stay pending.

options.label: Cap 5 attempts, library default on exhaustion
options.description: Set the same maximum attempt count (default 5, configurable) and rely on the library's default behavior when attempts are exhausted: the job sits in the failed set with no metric or alert. Retry cost is bounded with almost no code beyond a config value, and failed jobs remain inspectable. Con: nobody is told when jobs are exhausted, so the failed set grows unwatched. Effort human ~1 hour / CC ~5 min. R1, R2 fixed (D1, D2); R4-R8 stay pending.

options.label: No cap, as planned
options.description: Retry until success with no attempt limit and no terminal handling, as the plan currently reads. No config or monitoring work; a job eventually succeeds if its dependency ever recovers. Con: permanently broken jobs retry forever, consuming worker slots with no signal to anyone. Effort none. R1, R2 fixed (D1, D2); R4-R8 stay pending.

Question D3:
D3 — How many times do we retry, and what happens when we give up?
Project/branch/task: main branch, plan "Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md), all 5 workers.
ELI10: Exponential backoff says how long to wait between tries, but not when to stop. Without a cap, a job whose dependency is permanently broken retries forever, and nobody is told. The usual answer is a maximum number of attempts, after which the job is parked in a failed set (dead-letter) and an alert fires so a human can look at it in the morning.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either zombie jobs that retry for days and quietly eat worker capacity, or jobs that silently vanish into a failed set nobody watches.
Recommendation: A because a cap plus an exhaustion alert is the only option where a permanently failing job becomes a visible, bounded event.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Cap 5 attempts + dead-letter + alert (recommended) (human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Every job's retry cost is bounded and exhaustion becomes a visible metric per worker
  ✅ Dead-lettered jobs are inspectable and replayable from the library's failed set
  ❌ One more metric/alert to wire into the existing monitoring stack
B) Cap 5 attempts, library default on exhaustion (human: ~1 hour / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Retry cost is bounded with almost no extra code beyond a config value
  ✅ Failed jobs still land in the library's failed set for manual inspection
  ❌ Nobody is told when jobs are exhausted; the failed set grows unwatched
C) No cap, as planned (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ No config or monitoring work at all
  ✅ A job eventually succeeds if the dependency ever recovers
  ❌ Permanently broken jobs retry forever, consuming worker slots with no signal
Net: trading one metric and a config value against unbounded or invisible failure.
Header: Retry bounds
Options:
A) Cap 5 attempts + dead-letter + alert (recommended)
Set a maximum attempt count per worker type, default 5, configurable. When a job exhausts its attempts it lands in the library's failed/dead-letter set and a `job_retries_exhausted` metric/alert fires carrying the worker name and job id. Every job's retry cost is bounded, exhaustion is visible per worker, and dead-lettered jobs are inspectable and replayable. Con: one more metric/alert to wire into the existing monitoring stack. Retry until success with no attempt limit and no terminal handling, as the plan currently reads. No config or monitoring work; a job eventually succeeds if its dependency ever recovers.
